title: ‘Second again’ has been a soundtrack to Arsenal’s title bid – now it is being sung to Man City
content:
So, Pep Guardiola, how do you fancy your chances now? One last dramatic twist, perhaps? One act of self-sabotage from Arsenal to change the course of the 2025-26 Premier League title?

His team had done their bit, winning 3-0 against visitors Crystal Palace, and a song could be heard that has history for Manchester City, going all the way back to Roberto Mancini’s time as manager in the early 2010s. “We’ll fight to the end,” was the crowd’s message on Wednesday night, albeit not sung with quite the same conviction or volume that has been heard in previous years.

In ordinary circumstances, why not? The gap to Arsenal, at the top of the table, is back to two points, with two games each to play. If City can win at Bournemouth in their next league match on Tuesday, the drama will go to the final day of the season. And the lesson of history is that City have won five of their eight Premier League titles that way.

“The aim is to keep them (Arsenal) on their toes,” said City midfielder Phil Foden, after a victory that leaves his team with a superior goal difference to Arsenal, albeit by one (they are also now seven ahead for goals scored). “We’ve seen before that a lot of things can happen on the final day. I’ve experienced it many times when the game doesn’t go your way. We just have to keep pushing and doing our part.”

The problem for City, however, is a considerable one: that the fixtures have fallen so obligingly, to say the least, for a team with Arsenal’s needs.

First, Mikel Arteta’s side are at home on Monday against already-relegated Burnley. Then, on the final day of the Premier League season, they go to Selhurst Park to meet Palace, who will be playing in the UEFA Conference League final three days later. Nobody should expect Oliver Glasner to field many of his first-choice players in that one and, to be fair, who could blame him when Palace have the opportunity to win the first European final in their history?

Against that backdrop, there was no real tub-thumping from Guardiola after his team’s latest victory, especially when he contemplated the dangers associated with City’s last two league fixtures.

His eyes did sparkle when he was asked about Foden’s performance — the highlight being a beautifully measured backheel to set up the opening goal for Antoine Semenyo — and, again, when the subject turned to “the grandfather”, aka Bernardo Silva, who was playing potentially his penultimate game at the Etihad Stadium after nine years in City colours.

With his own future still unconfirmed, Guardiola could be seen pumping his fists in celebration when Rayan Cherki slipped in the third goal and, after the final whistle, there was a victory walk around the pitch and a lot of affectionate waving and kiss-blowing.

The reality, however, is that it would take something extraordinary now for the champions’ trophy to end up being adorned with blue ribbons not red. Extraordinary things do happen in football, as City know from experience, but Guardiola was noticeably reluctant to talk up his team’s chances.

“If we lose today, we know we have nothing to do (on the league season’s final day, May 24),” said the City manager. “We have (to win) to bring hope in the last game. But I would also say, wow, the next contender, Bournemouth, look at their form and what they have been doing this season. After that, Aston Villa (in the final game) with Unai Emery. They are not easy ones. We will focus, and let’s see what happens.”

His line-up last night told its own story, bearing in mind Cherki, Jeremy Doku and Erling Haaland all started the game on the bench, preserving their energy for Saturday’s FA Cup final against Chelsea.

Haaland was not required to enter the play as Guardiola prioritised that weekend trip to Wembley. “Chelsea have had a whole week at home, training and preparing for the final,” he pointed out. “We have to travel to London. They will be at home with their wives and kids, so that is (for us) fatigue, and fatigue, and fatigue.”

Some people may have misconstrued that as clear evidence that Guardiola, and City, have accepted the title race is over. The atmosphere at the Palace game was strangely subdued, to begin with, lacking the edge or jeopardy that would usually be associated at this stage of the season.

Ultimately, though, it all seemed perfectly logical once City had taken control and Omar Marmoush, playing instead of Haaland, doubled their lead shortly before half-time.

Those goals soothed the crowd’s mood and Guardiola sounded happy with his team’s work.

“In general, it was really, really good against a team that can always create problems,” he said. “(I’m) really pleased — three goals vs Brentford (in the previous match), three again here. I cannot ask for more. Now it’s a pleasure to go to the cathedral of English football, to play in the final, and hopefully we can get a better result than the last two times.”

That was a reference to losing the FA Cup final against Manchester United in 2024, and doing so again last year to Palace. Guardiola, like a lot of serial champions, tends to remember the bad results longer than the good ones. And there was a moment, an hour into this game, when the soundtrack was provided by the Palace fans. “Second again,” was the chorus, brutal and cutting in equal measures.

Second again? Everyone understood what those two words signified.

It was not so long ago, after all, that City supporters were blasting that song out as a celebration of Arsenal’s apparent ability to turn themselves from nearly men into genuine champions. Heck, every club’s supporters were taunting them this way. The schadenfreude was off the scale.

Now, though, the followers of Guardiola’s team may have to understand why it is being turned back on them.

Unless, of course, there is still one more twist to come.
